examples.ko: 요즘 아이 성적이 가장 큰 근심거리예요.
examples.en: These days my child's grades are my biggest worry.

examples.ko: 근심거리가 없으면 잠이 잘 올 텐데요.
examples.en: If I had no worries, I could sleep well.
For my parents, worrying about me was always a concern.

examples.ko: 근심거리를 혼자 안고 있지 말고 말해 보세요.
examples.en: Don't carry your worries alone, tell someone.
Now that the exam is over, one worry is gone.

examples.ko: 건강 문제가 요즘 새 근심거리로 생겼어요.
examples.en: A health problem has become a new worry lately.

explain: '걱정거리'와 거의 같은 뜻이에요. '근심'은 조금 글이나 점잖은 말투에 어울리고, 일상 대화에서는 '걱정거리'를 더 자연스럽게 느끼는 사람이 많아요.
explain_en: It is nearly the same as '걱정거리'. '근심' sounds a bit more written or formal, and many people find '걱정거리' more natural in everyday talk.

en: to be shocked; to be startled; to be astonished

examples.en: My younger sibling freaked out when he saw a cockroach.

examples.ko: 수도 요금이 너무 많이 나와서 기겁해서 전화했어요.
examples.en: The water bill was so high that I was shocked and called them.
The room was so messy it was shocking.
The child ran into his mother's arms in a fright.

examples.ko: 길에서 큰 개를 만나면 저는 항상 기겁해요.
examples.en: I always get terrified when I meet a big dog on the street.

examples.ko: 친구들이 기겁하지 않게 천천히 얘기해 주세요.
examples.en: Please speak slowly so that my friends don't get a shock.

explain: '놀라다'보다 훨씬 크게, 몸이 움찔할 만큼 놀랄 때 써요. 무서운 것, 징그러운 것, 예상 못 한 큰 금액 같은 데에 자주 써요. '기겁을 하다'라고 말하기도 하고, 편한 대화에서 잘 어울려요.
explain_en: It describes being startled much more strongly than '놀라다', enough to make your body jump. It is often used for scary or gross things, or an unexpectedly large amount of money. People also say '기겁을 하다', and it fits casual conversation well.

en: to be restless; to be nervous

examples.en: Waiting for the exam results, my mind is unsettled.
Last night's dreams were disturbing, so I slept badly.
The mood at the company is unsettled these days.

examples.ko: 뒤숭숭한 소문 때문에 일이 손에 안 잡혀요.
examples.en: Because of the unsettling rumors, I can't focus on work.
When my mind is uneasy, I take a walk.
I ended up spending the day feeling unsettled.

explain: 마음이나 꿈, 분위기가 불안하고 어수선할 때 써요. '어수선하다'는 정리 안 된 방이나 분위기에도 쓰지만, '뒤숭숭하다'는 마음이 불안하고 안정이 안 되는 느낌이 중심이에요.
explain_en: Use it when a mind, a dream or an atmosphere feels uneasy and unsettled. '어수선하다' can also describe a messy room or scene, but '뒤숭숭하다' centers on the anxious, unstable feeling.

en: to be pricking; to be tingling

examples.en: It stung when the needle went in.
I remembered the lie I told and felt a pang of guilt.

examples.ko: 친구가 내 이야기를 하는 것 같아서 뜨끔해요.
examples.en: It feels like my friend is talking about me, and I feel a pang of guilt.

examples.ko: 선생님이 숙제 얘기를 꺼내자 가슴이 뜨끔했어요.
examples.en: When the teacher brought up the homework, my heart skipped guiltily.
I twisted my ankle, and it stings every time I walk.

examples.ko: 야식을 먹다가 엄마와 눈이 마주쳐서 뜨끔했어요.
examples.en: I was eating a late-night snack and met Mom's eyes, and I felt caught.

explain: 몸이 찔리듯 순간 아플 때도 쓰고, 잘못한 게 들킬 것 같아서 마음이 찔릴 때도 써요. 두 번째 뜻은 '찔리다'와 가까워서 대화에서 아주 자주 나와요. 아픈 느낌이 계속될 때는 '뜨끔거리다'를 써요.
explain_en: It can mean a sudden sting in the body, and also the guilty prick you feel when you fear your mistake will be found out. The second meaning is close to '찔리다' and comes up a lot in conversation. For pain that keeps going, use '뜨끔거리다'.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 명예욕이 너무 강해서 늘 일등만 하려고 해요.
examples.en: He has such a strong desire for honor that he always wants to be first.
I drifted apart from my friend because of the hunger for fame.

examples.ko: 돈보다 명예욕이 더 큰 사람도 있어요.
examples.en: Some people care more about honor than money.
If you let go of the desire for honor, your mind feels much lighter.

examples.ko: 명예욕은 사람을 열심히 일하게 만들기도 해요.
examples.en: The desire for honor can also make people work hard.

examples.ko: 그는 명예욕에 눈이 멀어 거짓말까지 했어요.
examples.en: Blinded by the desire for honor, he even told lies.

explain: '권력욕', '식욕'처럼 '-욕'이 붙은 말과 같이 쓰여요. '명예욕이 강하다/크다'처럼 말하고, 지나치다는 느낌으로 쓰는 경우가 많아서 칭찬보다는 조금 비판하는 말투가 되기 쉬워요.
explain_en: It sits in the same family as words ending in '-욕' such as '권력욕' and '식욕'. People say '명예욕이 강하다/크다', and it often carries a feeling of excess, so it can sound more critical than complimentary.

examples.ko: 아이들은 모험심이 많아서 새로운 길로 가고 싶어 해요.
examples.en: Kids are adventurous, so they want to take new paths.
Out of a sense of adventure, I went backpacking alone.

examples.ko: 그 소설은 모험심 가득한 아이의 이야기예요.
examples.en: That novel is the story of a child full of adventure.

examples.ko: 동생은 모험심에 불타서 번지 점프에 도전했어요.
examples.en: My younger sibling, burning with a spirit of adventure, tried bungee jumping.

examples.ko: 나이가 들어도 모험심만은 잃고 싶지 않아요.
examples.en: Even as I get older, I don't want to lose my sense of adventure.

examples.ko: 여행지에서 모험심을 발휘해 낯선 음식을 먹어 봤어요.
examples.en: At the travel destination I got adventurous and tried unfamiliar food.

explain: '도전 정신'과 비슷하지만, 모험심은 낯설고 위험한 일을 해 보고 싶은 마음에 더 가까워요. '모험심이 강하다/많다/없다', '모험심을 키우다/자극하다'처럼 써요.
explain_en: It is similar to '도전 정신' (challenge spirit), but 모험심 is closer to the urge to try unfamiliar or risky things. It goes with '모험심이 강하다/많다/없다' and '모험심을 키우다/자극하다'.

examples.en: The blade has gone dull, so it doesn't cut well.

examples.ko: 매일 시끄러운 소리를 들었더니 소리에 무뎌졌어요.
examples.en: After hearing loud noise every day, I've grown numb to it.
As time passes, even sadness gradually dulls.
If you go through something again and again, you tend to become numb to the pain.
When the pencil lead gets blunt, you have to sharpen it again.

examples.ko: 요즘은 칭찬을 들어도 마음이 무뎌진 것 같아요.
examples.en: These days, even when I'm praised, my heart feels numb.

explain: 칼, 연필처럼 날카로운 물건에도 쓰고, 감각이나 감정이 둔해질 때도 써요. 감정에 쓸 때는 '~에 무뎌지다'처럼 무엇에 익숙해져서 느낌이 약해졌는지를 '에'로 말해요. 반대 느낌은 '날카로워지다'예요.
explain_en: It's used for sharp things like knives and pencils, and also when senses or feelings grow dull. For feelings, you mark what you've gotten used to with '에', as in '~에 무뎌지다'. The opposite feeling is '날카로워지다'.

en: to be ashamed; to be humiliated

examples.en: I felt embarrassed when my name was called out loudly.

examples.ko: 혼자 아무 말도 못 하니까 좀 무안해요.
examples.en: It's a bit awkward that I can't say anything.
Feeling awkward, I left the spot quickly.
When my gift was turned down, I got embarrassed and blushed.
I pretended not to notice so they wouldn't feel awkward.

examples.ko: 그렇게 말하면 상대가 무안할 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you say it like that, the other person might feel awkward.

explain: '무안하다'는 남 앞에서 어색하고 쑥스럽다는 뜻이에요. '부끄럽다'보다 상대방과의 관계에서 오는 어색함에 가까워요. 상대가 민망할까 봐 '무안하지 않게 해 주다'처럼 배려의 말로도 많이 써요.
explain_en: 무안하다 is feeling awkward or sheepish around others. It is closer to social awkwardness between people than 부끄럽다. A common considerate phrase is 무안하지 않게 해 주다 (to spare someone the awkwardness).

examples.en: The child saw me and gave a shy little smile.
She gave a little smile when she heard the compliment.
My younger sibling just smiled faintly without saying anything.

examples.ko: 그는 쑥스러운지 배시시 웃으며 고개를 숙였어요.
examples.en: He seemed embarrassed and bowed his head with a faint smile.

examples.ko: 아기가 배시시 웃는 모습이 너무 귀여워요.
examples.en: The way the baby smiles softly is so cute.

examples.ko: 뭐가 좋은지 하루 종일 배시시 웃고 있어요.
examples.en: For some reason she's been smiling to herself all day.

explain: '웃다'와 거의 같이 쓰이고, 소리 없이 입가만 살짝 웃는 모습을 그려요. 쑥스럽거나 기분이 좋을 때 어울리고, 큰 소리로 웃는 것에는 쓰지 않아요. 아이나 가까운 사람을 이야기할 때 귀엽고 다정한 느낌이 있어요.
explain_en: It almost always goes with '웃다' and pictures a soundless, slight smile at the corners of the mouth. It fits shy or happy moments, and not loud laughter. When talking about children or people close to you, it carries a cute, warm feel.

en: to be annoying; to be bothersome; to be tiresome

examples.en: Mosquitoes keep buzzing and it's so annoying.

examples.ko: 자꾸 오는 영업 전화가 성가셔서 받지 않아요.
examples.en: Sales calls keep coming and they're bothersome, so I don't answer.

examples.ko: 서류 절차가 복잡해서 성가신 일이 많아요.
examples.en: The paperwork is complicated, so there are many tiresome things.
My younger sibling kept following me, and it felt bothersome.
If it's not too much trouble, could you help me with this?

examples.ko: 하루에도 몇 번씩 오는 광고 문자가 성가셨어요.
examples.en: The ad messages that came several times a day were annoying.

explain: '귀찮다'와 비슷하지만 '성가시다'는 자꾸 신경 쓰이고 방해가 되는 느낌이 강해요. 부탁할 때 '성가시게 해서 죄송해요'처럼 정중하게 쓰기도 하고, 활용은 '성가셔요, 성가신'이에요.
explain_en: It is close to '귀찮다', but '성가시다' stresses the feeling of something repeatedly bothering or interrupting you. It is also used politely when asking favors, as in '성가시게 해서 죄송해요', and conjugates as '성가셔요, 성가신'.

examples.ko: 그렇게 성내지 말고 차분히 이야기해 봐요.
examples.en: Don't get so angry; let's talk calmly.

examples.ko: 아버지는 평소에 좀처럼 성내시는 일이 없어요.
examples.en: My father hardly ever gets angry.

examples.ko: 아이에게 성내고 나면 마음이 편하지 않아요.
examples.en: After I get angry at my child, I don't feel at ease.

examples.ko: 그는 작은 일에도 쉽게 성내서 친구가 별로 없어요.
examples.en: He gets angry easily over small things, so he has few friends.
I don't know why you're getting angry at me.

examples.ko: 화가 나도 성내기 전에 숨을 한 번 쉬어 보세요.
examples.en: Even when you're upset, take a breath before you lose your temper.

explain: '화내다'와 뜻이 가깝지만 일상 대화에서는 '화내다, 화를 내다'가 훨씬 자주 들려요. '성내다'는 조금 예스럽고 글이나 속담 같은 말투에서 더 어울려요. 윗사람이 화낼 때는 '성내시다'처럼 높여요.
explain_en: Its meaning is close to '화내다', but in everyday conversation '화내다' and '화를 내다' are heard far more. '성내다' sounds a bit old-fashioned and suits writing or proverb-like speech. For someone senior, you honor it as '성내시다'.

examples.en: My friends are jealous of my new bag.
The younger sister was jealous of her older sister's popularity.
Don't be jealous, and congratulate them together.
If you envy others, only your own heart gets tired.
A cold wind blows as if envying the spring.

examples.ko: 다들 시샘할 만큼 두 사람은 사이가 좋아요.
examples.en: The two get along so well that everyone is jealous.

explain: '친구를 시샘하다', '친구의 성공을 시샘하다'처럼 '을/를'과 함께 써요. '질투하다'보다 가볍게 샘내는 느낌이고, 연인 사이의 질투에는 '질투하다'가 더 자연스러워요. '봄을 시샘하는 추위'처럼 날씨에 비유해서도 써요.
explain_en: It takes an object with '을/를', as in '친구를 시샘하다' or '친구의 성공을 시샘하다'. It feels lighter than '질투하다', and for jealousy between lovers '질투하다' sounds more natural. It is also used figuratively for weather, as in '봄을 시샘하는 추위'.

examples.en: My little brother was being spiteful and hid the toy.

examples.ko: 친구가 상을 받으니까 괜히 심술이 났어요.
examples.en: When my friend won a prize, I felt a bit spiteful for no reason.
Don't be spiteful, let's play together.

examples.ko: 그 아이는 심술이 많아서 자주 혼나요.
examples.en: That child gets scolded often because he is so cranky.
Grandfather smiled with a mischievous look.
I have a friend who turns grumpy when hungry.

explain: 남이 잘되는 것이 샘나거나 일이 마음대로 안 될 때 괜히 비뚤어지게 구는 마음이에요. '심술을 부리다', '심술이 나다'로 자주 써요. 심술이 많은 사람은 '심술쟁이', 짓궂은 모습은 '심술궂다'라고 해요.
explain_en: It is the grumpy, contrary mood you get when you envy someone or things do not go your way. The common patterns are '심술을 부리다' (to act spiteful) and '심술이 나다' (to feel peevish). A peevish person is a 심술쟁이, and the adjective is 심술궂다.

examples.en: He nodded with a bitter smile.
After hearing my friend's words, I turned away with a bitter feeling.
I sighed bitterly when I saw the result.
My father just looked out the window with a bitter expression.

examples.ko: 그 소식에 씁쓸히 웃을 수밖에 없었어요.
examples.en: I could only give a bitter smile at the news.
The way he spoke so bitterly stays on my mind.

explain: '씁쓸하다'의 부사형으로, 서운하거나 허탈한 마음으로 하는 행동 앞에 와요. '씁쓸히 웃다'가 가장 잘 어울리고, 말할 때는 '씁쓸하게'도 많이 써요.
explain_en: This is the adverb form of '씁쓸하다', placed before actions done with a hurt or hollow feeling. '씁쓸히 웃다' is the most natural pairing, and in speech '씁쓸하게' is also common.

examples.ko: 동생은 새 신발이 더러워질까 봐 아까워해요.
examples.en: My younger sibling is reluctant to get the new shoes dirty.

examples.ko: 그는 돈 쓰는 것을 아까워하지 않아요.
examples.en: He doesn't begrudge spending money.
My mother felt it was a waste every time she threw away food.

examples.ko: 시간을 아까워하는 사람은 계획을 잘 세워요.
examples.en: People who value their time make good plans.

examples.ko: 친구는 비싼 우산을 잃어버리고 많이 아까워했어요.
examples.en: My friend lost an expensive umbrella and felt very sorry about it.

examples.ko: 너무 아까워해서 선물을 받고도 못 썼어요.
examples.en: I was so reluctant to use it that I couldn't, even after receiving the gift.

explain: '아깝다'는 내 마음을 말하고, '아까워하다'는 다른 사람이 아까운 마음을 보이는 모습을 말해요. 그래서 내 기분은 '아까워요', 남의 기분은 '아까워해요'라고 해요. 보통 '시간을', '돈을', '물건을'과 같이 써요.
explain_en: '아깝다' describes my own feeling, while '아까워하다' describes another person showing that feeling. So my feeling is '아까워요' and someone else's is '아까워해요'. It usually goes with objects such as '시간을', '돈을', and '물건을'.

examples.en: Test results depend on how you feel that day.
Vegetable prices can also be swayed by the weather.

examples.ko: 한 사람의 말에 좌우되지 말고 스스로 생각해 보세요.
examples.en: Don't be swayed by one person's words, and think for yourself.

examples.ko: 이번 경기는 첫 골에 좌우될 거예요.
examples.en: This match will be decided by the first goal.

examples.ko: 여행의 즐거움은 같이 가는 사람에 좌우됐어요.
examples.en: How much I enjoyed the trip depended on who I went with.
A life ruled by what others think is tiring.

explain: '~에 좌우되다'처럼 조사 '에'와 같이 써요. 어떤 일의 결과가 그것에 달려 있다는 느낌이에요. '달려 있다'는 일상 대화에서 더 자주 쓰고, 안 좋은 쪽으로 끌려다닐 때는 '휘둘리다'를 쓰기도 해요.
explain_en: It goes with the particle '에', as in '~에 좌우되다'. It feels like the outcome of something rests on that factor. '달려 있다' is more common in everyday talk, and '휘둘리다' is sometimes used when you are pushed around in a bad way.

examples.ko: 동생이 내 새 가방을 자꾸 탐내요.
examples.en: My younger sibling keeps coveting my new bag.

examples.ko: 그는 사장 자리를 탐내서 몰래 준비했어요.
examples.en: He coveted the boss's seat and prepared in secret.
You must not covet other people's things.

examples.ko: 그 선수는 우승을 탐냈지만 아쉽게 졌어요.
examples.en: That player wanted the title badly but sadly lost.
It's a position everyone wants, so competition is fierce.

examples.ko: 친구의 재능을 탐내지 말고 제 길을 가세요.
examples.en: Don't covet your friend's talent, just follow your own path.

explain: '남의 물건을 탐내다'처럼 대상을 목적어로 써요. 갖고 싶은 마음이 크고 욕심 같은 느낌이 있어서 좋은 뜻은 아니에요. 단순히 갖고 싶으면 '갖고 싶어 하다', 부러운 마음이면 '부러워하다'를 써요.
explain_en: The target is the object, as in 남의 물건을 탐내다. It carries a sense of greed, so it isn't a compliment. For simply wanting something, use 갖고 싶어 하다, and for envy use 부러워하다.

en: to be unreliable; to be groundless

examples.ko: 몇 년 준비한 일이 하루 만에 끝나서 너무 허망해요.
examples.en: Something I prepared for years ended in a day, and it feels so empty.

examples.ko: 열심히 모은 돈을 사기로 잃고 나니 허망했어요.
examples.en: After losing the money I worked hard to save to a scam, I felt hollow.

examples.ko: 허망한 마음에 한참 동안 하늘만 쳐다봤어요.
examples.en: Feeling empty, I just stared at the sky for a long time.

examples.ko: 인생이 허망하다는 생각이 들 때가 있어요.
examples.en: There are times when I feel that life is futile.

examples.ko: 그렇게 허망하게 지는 경기는 처음 봤어요.
examples.en: I've never seen a game lost so abruptly and pointlessly.

examples.ko: 너무 허망해서 아무 말도 나오지 않았어요.
examples.en: I felt so empty that I couldn't say a word.

explain: '허무하다'와 비슷하지만, '허망하다'는 기대하거나 애쓴 일이 갑자기 헛되게 끝났을 때 더 잘 어울려요. '허망하게 끝나다/지다'처럼 '허망하게' 형태로도 써요.
explain_en: It is similar to '허무하다', but '허망하다' fits best when something you hoped for or worked on ends suddenly in vain. It is also used in the form '허망하게', as in '허망하게 끝나다/지다'.

en: to confuse; to muddle; to mix up

examples.en: I sometimes mix up 'left' and 'right.'
You must not confuse public and private matters.

examples.ko: 두 사람을 혼동해서 이름을 잘못 불렀어요.
examples.en: I confused the two people and called the wrong name.
Because I mixed up the dates, I missed the appointment.

examples.ko: 소금과 설탕을 혼동하지 않게 이름을 써 두었어요.
examples.en: I wrote labels so I wouldn't confuse salt and sugar.
Many people confuse the twin brothers.

explain: 일상 대화에서는 '헷갈리다'를 더 많이 쓰고, '혼동하다'는 두 가지를 같은 것으로 잘못 보는 상황을 설명할 때 써요. '~와 ~를 혼동하다'처럼 두 대상을 함께 말해요. 반대로 나누어 알아보는 것은 '구별하다'예요.
explain_en: In daily talk 헷갈리다 is used more, while 혼동하다 is for explaining that two things are wrongly taken as the same. It takes both objects, as in ~와 ~를 혼동하다. The opposite, telling them apart, is 구별하다.

en: to be unclear; to be blurred

examples.en: I couldn't sleep, so my eyes look dull and unfocused.
I went into the meeting in a foggy state of mind.
He ended up giving a vague answer.
After taking the medicine, my head became foggy.
His attitude is so unclear that I don't know what he means.
That person's explanation stayed vague to the very end.

explain: 정신, 눈빛, 기억, 태도가 또렷하지 않을 때 써요. '흐리다'가 날씨나 유리에도 쓰이는 것과 달리, 이 말은 주로 사람의 상태나 태도에 써요.
explain_en: It is used when someone's mind, gaze, memory or attitude is not sharp or clear. Unlike '흐리다', which also fits weather or glass, this word mostly describes a person's state or attitude.

en: to be excited; to feel thrilled; to get worked up

examples.en: I'm so excited about going on a trip tomorrow.
I got more excited as the final approached.
He delivered the news in an excited voice.

examples.ko: 너무 흥분되어서 밤에 잠이 안 왔어요.
examples.en: I was so excited that I couldn't sleep at night.
I took a deep breath to calm my excited heart.

examples.ko: 흥분될 때는 천천히 말하는 게 좋아요.
examples.en: When you're worked up, it's good to speak slowly.

explain: '신나다', '설레다'는 기분 좋은 설렘이고, '흥분되다'는 기쁨뿐 아니라 화가 났을 때도 몸과 마음이 달아오르는 느낌이에요. 그래서 문맥을 보고 좋은 흥분인지 나쁜 흥분인지 알아야 해요.
explain_en: '신나다' and '설레다' are happy excitement; '흥분되다' is being worked up in body and mind, which can come from joy or from anger. Context tells you which.

dis.h: feel thrilled; a feeling comes over you

p.n: 흥분하다 is more active; 흥분되다 is the feeling itself.
